title: Coroner to raise concerns with FA over football’s cardiac arrest measures
content:
A coroner is to write to the Football Association to express her concerns that the sport is not doing enough to tackle the risks of players suffering cardiac arrest.

Valerie Charbit, assistant coroner of west London, said she would be filing a ‘Preventions of Future Deaths’ report citing the tragic circumstances in which Adam Ankers lost his life.

Ankers, 17, was playing for Wycombe Wanderers Foundation’s under-19s in February 2024 when he collapsed on the pitch and later died in hospital. The teenager, who harboured dreams of playing professionally, was later found to have had a genetic heart condition.

At an inquest, two years after his death, Charbit said she intended to contact English football’s governing body to raise her concern that “the FA’s SCA (sudden cardiac arrest) death training was not more widely disseminated or mandatory for all grassroots football coaches and referees”.

Charbit herself had undertaken the SCA course before conducting the week-long inquest, which was attended by representatives of the FA. However, the hearing was told that the referee of Ankers’ game had no training in this area and that it was the same for the coaches who were present on the day.

The coroner’s findings also noted her concern that “cardiac screening reduces the risk of death but is not available for all young football players”.

Ankers, a season-ticket holder at League One Wycombe, played as a right-back for the foundation team, based at Hendon College, and was described by Charbit as “a very admirable young man” with a bright future ahead of him.

His parents, Alistair and Naomi, were present at the inquest to hear the coroner say there had been “missed opportunities” to use an AED (automated external defibrillator), because the 999 emergency call handler had not recognised the signs of a cardiac arrest and advised against it while speaking to people on the scene.

“In a country where football is so well loved, it is, in my view, vital that there is a better understanding of when and how an AED can be used,” said Charbit.

Adjourning the inquest to April 14, Charbit said she would seek a reply from the FA and other interested parties within a two-week window and that will help her to determine what recommendations she makes in her final report.

An FA statement read: “We were deeply saddened to learn of the tragic passing of Adam Ankers in January 2024, and our thoughts remain with his family and loved ones. We have supported the coroner throughout the inquest, and we will fully review their findings and recommendations.”
